sentences.text: The woman came in the second week of September, on the ferry, with a stick.
Nél noticed her because she came down the harbour steps very slowly and then went and stood in front of the third bollard, which is what people did, and which meant something.
She stood there a long time.
Longer than anybody Nél had ever watched.
Then she picked up the shoe.
Nél was up on the wall by the ice machine and she got down and went along, which she would not normally have done, and stopped about four metres off, which was as close as she could make herself go.
The woman said, without turning round: "You'll be wanting to know." "Sorry." "Don't be.
If I were eleven and lived here I'd have been over quicker than that." She turned the shoe over in her hands.
She was perhaps eighty, and she was extremely well dressed, and she was not crying at all.
"It's mine," she said.
"I was twenty-two months old.

My mother had me on the wall in that pram there — well, not that one, but there — and she turned round for a matter of seconds and the pram went over the edge, brake and all." Nél did not say anything.
"They got me out.
Two men off a boat that shouldn't have been in that day.
My mother could not tell the story without stopping in the middle, so she stopped telling it, and I grew up knowing it the way you know a thing that is never described." She held up the shoe.
"One of these came off in the water.
She looked for it, apparently.
For years.
She used to say it as a joke and it was not a joke." "When was this?" "Nineteen forty-eight." The woman put the shoe back down on the third bollard.
Nél said, "Aren't you taking it?" And the woman looked at her, and looked at the shoe, and said something that Nél has repeated to people ever since and has never once had come out right.

She said: "It's been doing a job." Then she said that her mother had died in 1991 and had never known it had come back, and that she herself had only found out about the harbour and the bollard four months ago, from a cousin, at a funeral, in a conversation about something else entirely.
She stayed two nights and went back on the Thursday ferry.
Nél saw her once more, on the Wednesday evening, sitting outside the café with a coffee she was not drinking, looking at the water.
She did not go over.
She has wondered since whether she should have, and has concluded, most days, that she should not.
The shoe is still on the third bollard.
It has been moved twice since — once into the café and once, briefly and outrageously, into a display at the tourist office — and both times somebody put it back.

Nél is grown now and she works at the harbour, and about four times a year, after weather, there is something on the third bollard, and she is one of the three or four people who quietly makes sure the right person gets told.
She has never seen the gull do it.
Nobody has.
She has asked everybody.
She has stopped thinking that this is the interesting part.
